chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

agreed.text: Every elastic thing has a limit. Past it, the thing stays stretched or breaks.
agreed.evidence: Stretch a pen spring hard and it stays long. Engineers measure the limit of every material used in bridges and buildings.

agreed.text: A solid keeps its shape because of electric pulls and pushes between its atoms. Past the elastic limit, rows of atoms slip into new places.
agreed.evidence: X-rays show that the atoms in metals sit in neat rows. Electron microscopes show the slipped rows inside metal that was bent too far.

agreed.text: A stretched or squashed elastic thing stores energy, which it gives back when it springs back.
agreed.evidence: Catapults, bows, wind-up clocks and bouncing balls all use it. Scientists measure the energy that goes in and comes out.

agreed.text: Earthquakes happen when bent rock underground suddenly slips and springs back.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured how the ground had bent before and after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Today GPS stations measure rock slowly bending across the Himalaya.

challenging.claim: Stretchy things are weak, and strong things are stiff.
challenging.for: A rubber band breaks easily, while a steel rod does not stretch at all that we can see.
challenging.against: Spider silk is very stretchy and, weight for weight, stronger than steel wire. Living roots and bamboo survive storms because they bend. Being able to stretch can make a thing tougher, because it soaks up a sudden push instead of cracking.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only stiff things can be strong.

challenging.claim: Hooke's rule works for every springy thing.
challenging.who: Robert Hooke himself, in 1678, and many people since
challenging.for: Hooke found equal steps in metal springs, long wires and dry wood, and said the rule held for every springy body. Steel springs follow the rule very closely for small stretches.
challenging.against: Rubber bands follow it only roughly. Their steps often grow as the band gets long. And every spring breaks the rule once it is pulled past its elastic limit. Then the steps stop being equal, and the spring stays long. Hooke's rule is very useful, but it is a rule for small stretches.
challenging.context: Robert Hooke found a rule for how springs stretch. This card asks whether his rule always works.

challenging.claim: Robert Hooke alone discovered the rule for springs, and invented the spring for watches.
challenging.for: Hooke published the spring rule in 1678. He also worked on springs to control watches in the 1660s.
challenging.against: Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist, built a watch with a spiral spring in 1675. Hooke said he had the idea first, and the two men argued bitterly. Historians still disagree about who was first with the watch spring. The spring rule is fairly given to Hooke. In France, Edme Mariotte found the same rule on his own a few years later.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering how springs work.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton had the only portrait of Robert Hooke destroyed.
challenging.who: A story often told about Hooke and Newton, who were rivals
challenging.for: No portrait of Hooke survives from his lifetime. Newton disliked Hooke. After Hooke died, Newton led the Royal Society, the science club where a portrait might have hung.
challenging.against: Nobody has found any evidence that Newton destroyed a portrait. It may simply have been lost. In the 2000s an artist, Rita Greer, painted new portraits of Hooke from written descriptions of him.
challenging.context: Robert Hooke found the rule for how springs stretch. This card is about a story of why we do not know what he looked like.

challenging.claim: Rubber was invented in Europe or America, by people like Charles Goodyear.
challenging.for: Charles Goodyear found in 1839 how to make rubber tough with heat and sulphur. That made car tyres and rubber bands possible.
challenging.against: About 3,500 years ago, people in Mexico and Central America were already making bouncy rubber balls. In 1999, Dorothy Hosler and her team at MIT showed how. They mixed the milky sap of the rubber tree with juice from a morning glory vine. Different mixtures made rubber that bounced more, or rubber that was tougher.
challenging.context: This card is about who first made rubber, the stuff of rubber bands and bouncy balls.

challenging.claim: Cold would not matter to the rubber seals on the space shuttle Challenger.
challenging.who: Managers at NASA and at the company that made the booster rockets, in January 1986
challenging.for: The seals had worked on earlier flights. The managers were under pressure to launch on time.
challenging.against: An engineer called Roger Boisjoly warned the night before that cold rubber goes stiff and springs back too slowly. The launch went ahead on a freezing morning. A seal failed, and the shuttle broke apart. The seven astronauts on board died. Later, the scientist Richard Feynman squeezed a piece of the seal rubber in a small clamp. He dipped it in iced water during the inquiry. When he let go, it stayed squashed for a few seconds instead of springing back.
challenging.context: This card is a sad true story. It shows why it matters how fast rubber springs back.

challenging.claim: A branch that is bending is about to break.
challenging.for: Branches do break when they are bent too far.
challenging.against: Bending by itself is safe. A green branch bends in every breeze and springs back. The warning sign is a branch that bends and does not come all the way back. That means it has passed its elastic limit. Engineers watch for this same sign in cranes and bridges.
challenging.context: This card is about how to tell when something that bends is in danger, and when it is fine.

big_questions.q: A spring lying on the table looks as if nothing is happening inside it. Is anything going on in there?
big_questions.hint: Think of each atom resting where the pushes and pulls from its neighbours balance. What happens to them when you stretch it?

big_questions.q: Why should equal handfuls of coins give equal steps of stretch? What would have to be true inside the band?
big_questions.hint: What if the band pulls back a little harder for each centimetre it is stretched?

big_questions.q: Is anything completely stiff? Does a brick stretch even a tiny bit when you stand on it?
big_questions.hint: Hooke saw a long wire stretch when a short one seemed not to. How could you show a brick bending?

big_questions.q: When you stretch a catapult, where is the energy while you are holding it? Where does it go after you let go?
big_questions.hint: Think of the atoms pulled out of their resting places, and then the flying paper ball.

big_questions.q: After a big pull, the pen spring rests at a new length, and springs back to that. Is it the same spring as before?
big_questions.hint: All its atoms are still there. What has changed is which atoms hold which.

big_questions.q: Rock under the Himalaya is being bent a little every year, and nobody can see it. How can anyone know that something is storing strain before it breaks?
big_questions.hint: Think of a branch that stays a little bent after a swing. What do GPS stations measure?

big_questions.q: A flea, a kangaroo and you all use springs to move. Why might living things have ended up so full of springs?
big_questions.hint: A spring gives back most of the energy you put in. Why would that help an animal that runs or jumps every day?

big_questions.q: Space itself stretches. What could space be made of, that it can stretch?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows. What would you guess, and how could anyone ever test it?

big_questions.q: People in Mexico made bouncy rubber 3,500 years ago, but the books often credit someone else. Why do some inventors get remembered and others get forgotten?
big_questions.hint: Who wrote the books? Who was allowed to write?

big_questions.q: An engineer warned that cold rubber would not spring back fast enough, and the launch went ahead. How should people decide when a test result means 'stop'?
big_questions.hint: Later, the scientist Richard Feynman showed it with a piece of the rubber and a glass of iced water. What made his test so hard to argue with?

story.title: The Tired Branch
story.note: Rubber tapping in Kerala, smoked rubber sheets and the Onam swing, the oonjal, are real. Ammu, her family, Biju and the mango tree are made up. The warning sign in the story is real physics: a branch or spring that no longer springs all the way back has gone past its elastic limit, and may soon break.
text: In a village near Kottayam, in Kerala, the rubber trees stand in long straight rows, like children lined up for school. Every morning before the sun was up, Ammu's mother walked between them with a lamp on her forehead and a curved knife in her hand. On each tree she shaved a thin spiral strip of bark. Out of the cut crept a white, slow milk, which ran down the spiral into a coconut-shell cup. Latex, her mother called it. Once it dried, it would be rubber.

Ammu was ten. Her job came after school. She carried the full cups home, poured the latex into flat trays and helped her mother squeeze it into sheets through the iron rollers in the shed. Then the sheets were hung in the smoke above the fire to dry, brown and shining, like enormous dosas.

Before any sheet was sold, her mother tested it. She took one corner between her finger and thumb and pulled. A good sheet stretched, and then, when she let go, slid back flat as if nothing had happened. Once Ammu found an old sheet that had been forgotten in the sun for weeks. When her mother pulled it, it stretched and stayed stretched, a tired little bulge. When she pulled again, it tore.
'See,' said her mother. 'When it stops coming back, it is close to breaking.'
Ammu said yes, Amma, the way you say yes to things you are not really listening to. It was August, and Onam was coming, and Onam meant the swing.

Every year the children of the lane hung an oonjal, a festival swing, from the big mango tree at the end of the path. It was a plank seat on two long ropes, decorated with marigolds and mango leaves. This year Biju, who was twelve and the leader of everything, had a plan. 'The low branch is for babies,' he said. 'We'll use the high one. The swing will go up past the roof of the shed.'
The high branch was thinner. It stuck out over the path like an arm reaching for something. Biju climbed up and knotted the ropes round it, and everyone cheered.

On the first day, the swing was glorious. When Biju swung, the branch bent down under him like a fishing rod, and lifted him up again, so that every swing had an extra bounce at the bottom. The children shrieked. They queued all afternoon. Ammu had three turns. At the top of each one she could see over the shed and across the whole green sea of rubber trees, and her stomach floated up into her throat.
On the second day, the bigger children started swinging two at a time, standing up, pumping as hard as they could. 'Higher!' they yelled. 'Make it fly!'
Ammu was waiting her turn when she noticed something. When the two big girls jumped off, the swing hung still. And the branch did not go all the way back up.

She looked again. In the morning, the swing's plank had hung level with her chin. Now it hung level with her shoulder. The branch had bent and stayed bent, just a little, the way the old rubber sheet had stretched and stayed stretched.
She went cold all over, even in the August heat.
'Biju,' she said. 'The branch is tired.'
Biju laughed. Everyone laughed. 'It's a strong branch,' he said. 'It bounced me all day yesterday.'
'It bounced back yesterday,' said Ammu. 'It isn't bouncing back now. Look at the seat. It's lower.'

'You're scared because you're small,' said one of the big girls, and the others made chicken noises. Ammu's face went hot. She wanted to be quiet. Being quiet would have been much easier. But she thought of the old sheet, the tired bulge, and the sound it made when it tore.
Her little sister Kunju was next in the queue, holding up her arms to be lifted on.
'No,' said Ammu, and she pulled Kunju back by her frock, so hard that Kunju began to cry.
'Fine,' said Biju. 'Then I'll show you.' He climbed onto the plank, stood up, and pumped once, twice, three times, swinging higher than the shed roof.
On the fourth swing there was a sound like a coconut splitting.

The branch did not snap all at once. It cracked, and sagged, and Biju, at the bottom of the swing, felt the ropes go soft in his hands. He jumped. He landed on his knees in the mud of the path. A second later the whole branch, ropes, marigolds and all, came down with a heavy, leafy crash exactly where Kunju would have been sitting.
Nobody said anything for a long time. A crow, offended, flew off into the rubber trees.
Biju stood up slowly. His knees were muddy and his face was white. He looked at the broken branch, with its pale, splintered end. Then he looked at Ammu.
'How did you know?' he said.

Ammu told him about the sheet. She showed him how the swing had hung lower and lower. 'When something stops coming back,' she said, 'it's near the end.' She didn't say 'I told you.' She didn't need to.

That evening, Ammu's mother walked down the lane and looked at the branch on the ground. She looked at the high stump, and at the low, thick branch that the swing had always hung from before. She did not scold anyone. She only touched Ammu's head on her way home, very lightly.

The next morning, the children hung the swing again, on the low branch. It was not as exciting. It did not go higher than the shed. But after every turn, Ammu watched the seat as the rider jumped off, and every time, the branch lifted it back up to exactly the height of her chin.
On Onam day, Biju pushed Kunju on the swing himself, gently, for nearly an hour.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a branch, like a rubber band or a spring, is elastic. Pushed a little, it bends and springs all the way back. Pushed past its elastic limit, it bends and stays bent. That small bend that does not come back is the warning. The thing has started to change inside, and it is close to breaking. Ammu spots this because she has seen the same thing in an old rubber sheet. Engineers watch for this sign in bridges, cranes and aeroplane wings.
ask: How did Ammu's mother test a rubber sheet? What did it mean when the sheet stayed stretched?
What did Ammu notice about the swing seat after the big children jumped off?
Why did the branch break on the second day, but not on the first?
Why was it hard for Ammu to speak up? What helped her?
Have you ever seen something that 'stopped coming back'? A rubber band, a spring or a toy? What happened to it next?
art: Dawn in a Kerala rubber plantation, a woman with a head lamp shaving a spiral cut on a tree, white latex running into a coconut-shell cup.
Brown rubber sheets hanging in the smoke of a shed, and Ammu's mother pulling a corner of one between finger and thumb.
An Onam swing decorated with marigolds hanging from a high, thin mango branch, children queueing below.
Ammu staring at the empty swing seat, which now hangs at her shoulder, the branch bent lower than before.
The branch cracking and falling with its ropes and flowers, Biju landing in the mud, Ammu holding her little sister back.
The swing hung again from the low, thick branch, Ammu watching the seat rise back to the height of her chin.

games.title: Spring Back, Stay or Snap?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out
items: TEST IT: stretch a rubber band a little and let go. What does it do?
TEST IT: squeeze a ball of chapati dough. Does it spring back?
TEST IT: bend a plastic ruler a little and let go. What does it do? Don't bend it far, or it may snap.
TEST IT: pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: if you stretch, squash or bend this thing, will it spring back, stay changed, or snap? Put the card on that mat.
Then name one place where that thing is useful because it behaves that way. A good idea wins one spring token.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test together. The first person to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor labelled SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP, with a pile of face-down cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats and put the cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says 'Rubber band' over the SPRING BACK mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card and put it on a mat.

setup.art: Children doing a TEST IT card, one stretching a rubber band, one pressing dough.
setup.caption: 3. TEST IT cards: everyone tries it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor: SPRING BACK, STAY and SNAP. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down in a pile. 3. Put the spring tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Here are three mats. Spring back, stay changed and snap. Before we start, can you think of one thing for each mat? Why does it belong there?
flow.kid: Put the three mats on the floor. Spring back, stay, and snap. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, pick a mat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the card game Spring Back, Stay or Snap. It is a game about which things are elastic. Here you set up the game.

ask.q: Name one thing for each mat, and say why.
good: A hair band springs back, because it goes back to its loop.
Playdough stays changed.
A papad snaps.

flow.do: Find the card 'Pen spring, pulled very hard'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with a tricky one. A pen spring, pulled very hard. Does it spring back, stay, or snap?
flow.kid: Practice card: a pen spring, pulled very hard. Spring back, stay or snap? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why does a spring pulled very hard stay long?
good: It went past its limit.
It was stretched too far, so it can't come back.

check.q: A pen spring pulled very hard. Which mat does it go on?
check.why: Game moment: STAY is right. Pulled gently, the spring would go on SPRING BACK. Pulled very hard, it passes its elastic limit and stays long. Picking SNAP usually means 'too far' is pictured as always breaking. Springs usually stretch out first.

flow.parent: The same spring pulled gently goes on SPRING BACK. This shows that one thing can be elastic up to a limit, and then stay changed.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They name a place where that behaviour is useful. 3. Give one token for each good idea.
flow.say: Put your card on a mat. Then tell me one place where it helps that this thing springs back, stays or snaps.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Then say where that is useful. Each good idea wins a 🌀 token.
flow.parent: Good ideas: a hair band must spring back, or it would fall off. Playdough must stay, or you could not make shapes. A papad snapping is how you know it is crisp. Some cards are tricky. A sponge springs back. Crumpled foil stays. A spider web springs back, which is how it catches flies without breaking.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll try it and see who was right.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: You pinched the skin on your hand. Why did it spring back?
good: Skin is elastic.
It has stretchy stuff inside it, called elastin.

flow.think: Can one thing be on two mats? When?

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Then look at the three piles together.
flow.say: Look at the three piles. Which pile is biggest? Which things were the hardest to decide?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now look at the piles. Which things were hard to decide? Why?
flow.think: Steel, glass and stone are a little elastic too. Do you think anything is never elastic at all?

games.context: This is a card game about elastic things. Elastic means a thing springs back to its shape when you let go. For each thing on a card, players decide: does it spring back, stay changed, or snap?

games.title: Human Springs
games.players: 2 to 6 players, with one grown-up as the caller

printables.title: 16 caller cards
items: STIFF SPRING: move only half as far
FLOPPY SPRING: move twice as far
COLD RUBBER: spring back very slowly
TOO FAR! You pass your limit and stay where you are
TOO FAR! You snap and sit down
STORE IT: crouch and hold, then jump on 'Let go!'

rules: Each player is a spring. Stand on a spot marked with a chappal. That is your resting place.
The caller reads a card. For each gentle pull, the spring takes one step forward. For each gentle push, it takes one step back.
On 'Let go!', every spring jumps back to its resting place.
Special cards change the rules for one round, like STIFF SPRING or TOO FAR.
A spring that moves the wrong number of steps sits out one round. Play until every card has been read.

setup.art: Children standing in a line, each beside a chappal on the floor marking their resting place.
setup.caption: 1. Each spring stands by its chappal.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while a child takes two big steps forward.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads a card. Springs move that many steps.

setup.art: The children jumping back to their chappals as the caller shouts 'Let go!'.
setup.caption: 3. On 'Let go!', everyone springs back.

flow.do: 1. Put one chappal on the floor for each player, in a line with space in front. 2. Each player stands beside a chappal. 3. Shuffle the caller cards.
flow.say: You are all springs. Your chappal is where you rest. When I pull, you stretch forward. When I push, you squash back. When I say 'Let go', you spring home.
flow.kid: You are a spring! Stand by your chappal. That is your home. A pull means step forward. Let go means jump home.
flow.context: This is the first step of Human Springs, an acting game. Each player pretends to be a spring that stretches, squashes and springs back. The founder of DeepKids suggested this game.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Check that each spring moves the right number of steps: one pull, one step.
flow.say: Two gentle pulls! Now let go! Did everyone spring all the way home?
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. One pull, one step. Two pulls, two steps. Let go means jump home!

ask.q: Three pulls made you move three steps. What would six pulls do?
good: Six steps.
Twice as far.

flow.parent: This acts out the spring rule: double the pull, double the stretch. Robert Hooke wrote this rule down in 1678.

flow.do: Read the special cards: STIFF SPRING, FLOPPY SPRING, COLD RUBBER, TOO FAR and STORE IT.
flow.say: Too far! You've passed your limit. When I say let go, you can't get home. You stay where you are.
flow.kid: Special card! A stiff spring moves only a little. Too far means you can't get home. Act it out!

check.q: A spring is pulled TOO FAR, past its limit. When you let go, what happens?
options: It springs all the way back
It stays stretched, or it snaps
check.why: Game moment: a spring pulled past its limit cannot get home. It stays stretched or snaps. Picking 'springs all the way back' means elastic was thought to have no limit. Picking 'shorter' mixes up stretching with squashing.

flow.parent: COLD RUBBER links to a true story. Cold rubber springs back slowly. That mattered on the space shuttle Challenger in 1986. Tell it only if your child is ready for a sad story.

flow.do: Finish with STORE IT and BOUNCE. Everyone crouches, holds, then jumps on 'Let go!'.
flow.say: Crouch down and hold it. You are a squashed spring, full of stored energy. Let go!
flow.kid: Crouch low and hold. You are a squashed spring. Wait for it. Let go! Jump!
flow.think: When you crouch before a jump, your legs are like springs. Where in your body are the springs?

games.context: This is an acting game. Each child is a spring. They stretch when the caller pulls, squash when the caller pushes, and spring back home on 'Let go!'.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, says: 'Only soft things are elastic. Hard things never spring back.' Which thing shows she is wrong?
opts: The hard steel spring inside a clicky pen
A soft pillow
A lump of playdough
A cotton ball
items.why: A steel spring is hard, but it springs back every time you click the pen. So elastic does not mean soft. Picking the pillow agrees with Kavya, because a pillow is soft. Playdough is soft and does not spring back at all.
items.art: A clicky pen opened up, showing its small steel spring.

items.p: Sort these. After you let go, does each one spring back, stay changed, or snap?
items.a: see items
items.why: Sponges and hair bands are elastic. Playdough and foil keep their new shape. A papad and a glass bangle hardly bend before they break.

items.p: An elastic thing changes shape when you push or pull it. When you let go, it goes ____ to its old shape.
items.why: Elastic needs both parts: it changes shape, and then it goes back. Playdough changes shape too, but it does not go back, so it is not elastic.

items.p: You hang a paper cup from a rubber band. With 5 coins in the cup, the band is 11 cm long. With 10 coins, it is 12 cm. What is the best guess for 15 coins?
opts: About 13 cm
Still 12 cm
About 24 cm
Shorter, about 10 cm
items.why: Each 5 coins added about 1 cm, so 5 more coins should add about 1 cm more. 12 + 1 = 13 cm. Picking 24 cm means doubling the length, but only the coins went up by one step. Picking 'shorter' comes from thinking the band fights back. It does pull back, but it still gets longer.
items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: In the coin stretch test, we add coins in equal handfuls of 5. Why not add 3 coins one time and 8 the next?
items.a: A strong answer says that equal steps let you compare. If each step is the same 5 coins, you can see whether each step adds the same stretch. With 3 and then 8, you could not tell if the band was following a pattern.
items.why: Equal steps make a pattern easy to see. This is what made the line on the graph straight.
items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: The further a rubber band is stretched, the harder it pulls back.
items.why: True. You can feel it in your fingers. The band stops stretching at the point where its pull back is as strong as the pull of the coins. More coins, so the band stretches further, until its pull back matches again.

items.p: A girl pulls a pen spring very hard. Now it stays long and loose. She says, 'It is more elastic now, because it is longer.' What is wrong with her idea?
opts: The spring went past its elastic limit, so it no longer springs back properly
Nothing. Longer springs are always more elastic
The spring got heavier, so it hangs lower
Pen springs are not elastic at all
items.why: Elastic means springing back, not being long. She pulled the spring past its elastic limit. Now it stays stretched, so it is less elastic, not more. Picking 'not elastic at all' misses that it sprang back when it was pulled gently.
items.context: In the Find the Limit experiment, you stretch different things, let go, and measure them again.

items.p: In this unit's story, a girl called Ammu watches a festival swing on a mango branch. In the morning the seat hangs at her chin. After the big children swing hard, it hangs at her shoulder. Why is that a warning?
opts: The branch bent and stayed bent, so it had passed its elastic limit and might break
The ropes got longer in the hot sun
Ammu had grown taller that day
A lower swing is always safer
items.why: A branch that springs all the way back is still elastic. One that stays bent has gone past its limit, and that comes just before breaking. Picking the ropes is a fair guess, but the story says the branch was what had sagged.
items.context: In the story The Tired Branch, children in Kerala hang an Onam swing from a thin, high mango branch.

items.p: Match each spring to its job.
pairs: squash and push your body back up
soak up the bumps in the road
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Springs are used wherever something must push back, pull back, or soak up a bump.

items.p: In the Band Launch, you pull a rubber band back 5 cm and it flies 1 metre. Next you pull it back 15 cm. What will most likely happen?
opts: It flies further, because a longer stretch stores more energy
It flies the same 1 metre, because it is the same band
It flies less far, because it is tired
It does not fly at all
items.why: A longer stretch puts more energy into the band. When you let go, the band gives that energy back as movement, so it flies further. Picking 'the same' pictures the band as having one fixed push. Its push depends on how far it is stretched.
items.context: In the Band Launch, you hook a rubber band over the 0 end of a ruler, pull it back, let go, and measure how far it flies.

items.p: Put the steps of a rubber ball's bounce in order, from first to last.
items: The ball falls towards the floor
The bottom of the ball squashes flat
The ball springs back round and pushes on the floor
items.a: order shown
items.why: A bounce is a squash and then a spring back. The squash happens too fast to see, but a wet ball leaves a round mark that shows how flat it went.

items.p: In the Bounce Test, a rubber ball bounces back up, but a ball of dough just goes splat. Explain why.
items.a: A strong answer says the rubber ball squashes and then springs back, and the spring back pushes it up. The dough squashes and stays squashed. It never springs back, so nothing pushes it up again.
items.why: A bounce needs an elastic squash. Being heavy or round does not matter: a heavy rubber ball still bounces.
items.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop different balls from 1 metre and see how high each one bounces back.

items.p: Think of two springy things you found in your Spring Hunt. For each one, say what would go wrong if it stopped springing back.
items.a: Two real finds, each with what would go wrong. For example: if my hair band stopped springing back, it would hang loose and fall out. If the spring in the clothes peg stopped, the peg would not grip and the clothes would blow away.
items.why: Asking 'what would go wrong?' shows the job each spring does.

items.p: Draw a rubber band held between two fingers, first loose and then stretched. On the stretched one, draw arrows showing which way the band pulls on each finger.
items.a: Two drawings: a small loop, then a long loop. On the long loop, the arrows point inwards, towards the middle of the band, because the band pulls back towards its old shape.
items.why: A stretched band always pulls back towards its old shape. You can feel this pull on your fingers.
items.art: Two fingers holding a rubber band, with space to draw arrows.

items.p: In the story The Tired Branch, the children of a lane in Kerala hang an Onam swing from a mango tree. They must choose a branch. Three people say what they think.

views.says: Use the high, thin branch. It bends more, so every swing gets an extra bounce and goes higher.
Use the low, thick branch. It bends less, so it stays far away from its elastic limit.

views.who: Ammu's mother, who tests rubber sheets
views.says: Either branch can be used if you check it. Every day, see if the seat comes back to the same height.

items.ask: Which branch would you choose? Give a reason using the words bend, spring back or elastic limit. Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: A strong answer picks a branch and explains it with springing back. A thin branch bends more, which gives a bouncier swing, but it gets near its limit sooner. A thick branch bends less and is safer, but less exciting. The best answers admit the other side and may add a check, like watching the seat height every day.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Springiness is fun, and safety matters. Watching whether a thing still springs all the way back is how you know it is safe.

items.p: Look at this graph from a coin stretch test. Where does the pattern change?
opts: After 20 coins, each 5 coins add more than 1 cm
At 5 coins, the band stops stretching
The pattern never changes
At 0 coins, the band is too long
items.why: Up to 20 coins the line is straight: each 5 coins add 1 cm. After 20 coins the steps jump to 2 cm and then 3 cm. That is a sign the band is near its elastic limit. Picking 'never changes' means only the first part of the line was read.

chart.title: Made-up example: a rubber band pulled past its limit
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Up to 20 coins, each 5 coins add 1 cm. After that the steps get bigger.

items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: A pen spring is 4 cm long. With 1 small weight hanging on it, it is 5 cm. With 2 weights, it is 6 cm. If the pattern holds, with 4 weights it will be ____ cm.
items.why: Each weight adds 1 cm. 4 weights add 4 cm. 4 + 4 = 8 cm. This only works below the elastic limit. Hang too much and the pattern breaks.

items.p: A shopkeeper in Madurai makes a weighing hook for mangoes from a rubber band. A thin band stretches 10 cm with one mango and snaps with three. A thick band stretches 3 cm with one mango. Which band should she use?
opts: The thick band, because it is stiffer and stays below its limit with heavy loads
The thin band, because a bigger stretch is always better
Either band, because all bands are the same
Neither, because rubber cannot weigh things
items.why: A stiff band needs a bigger pull to stretch. So three mangoes keep it below its elastic limit, and it will spring back every time. Picking the thin band is tempting, because its stretch is easy to see. But it snaps before the job is done.

items.p: One rubber band stretches 4 cm with 20 coins. Now two of the same bands hang side by side, holding the same 20 coins together. About how far do they stretch?
opts: About 2 cm
About 4 cm
About 8 cm
items.why: Side by side, the two bands share the coins. Each one carries only half, so each stretches about half as far: 2 cm. Picking 8 cm means picturing the two stretches adding up. That happens only when the bands are joined in a chain.
items.context: In the Two in a Row activity, you hang the same coins from one band, from two bands in a chain, and from two bands side by side.

items.p: A perfect rubber ball, dropped from 1 metre, would bounce back higher than 1 metre.
items.why: False. Even a perfect ball could only come back to where it started. Real balls lose some energy as heat and sound at each squash, so they always come back lower. A ball can only go higher if someone throws it down.

items.p: Look at these Bounce Test results. A friend says the sponge ball is the most elastic, because it is the softest. What do the results show?
opts: The rubber ball is most elastic, because it springs back highest
Your friend is right: the sponge ball is most elastic
The dough ball is most elastic
All the balls are equally elastic
items.why: The rubber ball came back up 80 cm out of 100 cm, so it springs back best. The sponge ball came back only 20 cm. Soft is not the same as elastic. Your friend's guess is common, which is why testing matters.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

items.context: In the Bounce Test, you drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high each one bounces back.

items.p: Sort these by how they store energy.
items: the rubber band car, wound up
items.a: see items
items.why: A catapult band, a bow string and trampoline springs are pulled longer. A pen spring and a landing ball are pressed shorter. The car's band is twisted round the axle.

items.p: A rubber band car goes 60 cm with 5 winds and 180 cm with 15 winds. About how far will it go with 10 winds?
opts: About 120 cm
About 60 cm
About 240 cm
About 10 cm
items.why: Each wind adds about 12 cm: 60 divided by 5 is 12. 10 winds is 10 times 12, which is 120 cm. It sits halfway between 60 and 180. Picking 240 cm means going past 15 winds instead of between.
items.context: In the Rubber Band Car project, you twist a rubber band round the back axle by winding the wheels backwards.

items.p: A girl tests her rubber band car twice. She winds it 5 times on a carpet, then 15 times on a smooth tiled floor. She says, 'The extra winds made it go further.' What is wrong with her test? How would you fix it?
items.a: A strong answer says two things changed at once: the number of winds and the floor. The tiles may have let the car roll further. To fix it, she should test both on the same floor and change only the winds.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Then you know what caused the difference.
items.context: In the Rubber Band Car project, you twist a rubber band round the back axle by winding the wheels backwards.

items.p: In the Rubber Band Orchestra, you stretch one band tighter round the box and pluck it again. What happens to the sound?
opts: The note goes higher
The note goes lower
The note stays the same
It makes no sound
items.why: A tighter band pulls back harder, so it springs back and forth faster. Faster shaking, called vibrating, makes a higher note. A veena or guitar player tightens a string to make it higher in the same way.
items.context: In the Rubber Band Orchestra, you stretch rubber bands round a box and pluck them.

items.p: Match each living being to the springy part they use.
pairs: a springy pad that flings them into a jump
long tendons that stretch and spring back as they hop
a stretchy silk web that catches flies without breaking
a springy backbone that bends and springs back as they run
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Living beings store energy in springy parts and get it back. This saves effort when they jump, hop or run.

items.p: After a storm in Mysuru, a clump of bamboo is still standing. But an old, dry branch nearby has snapped. Explain why one bent and one broke.
items.a: A strong answer says the green bamboo is elastic. It bends in the wind, stores the push for a moment, and springs back. The dry branch is brittle. It cannot bend much, so the push breaks it.
items.why: Bending lets a thing soak up a sudden push. This is why green twigs bend and dry twigs snap in the Bend or Snap activity.

items.p: A hanging luggage scale has a spring inside. Why does a heavier bag move the pointer further? And why would a far too heavy bag ruin the scale?
items.a: A strong answer says a heavier bag pulls harder, so the spring stretches further and the pointer moves further. A far too heavy bag would pull the spring past its elastic limit. Then the spring would stay stretched, and every reading after that would be wrong.
items.why: The scale only works while the spring follows the rule: a bigger pull, a bigger stretch, and back again.

items.p: Draw the catapult from the Catapult Challenge, pressed down and ready to fire. Label where the energy is stored before you let go.
items.a: A drawing of the catapult with the arm pressed down. The label points to the bent stick or the stretched rubber bands.
items.why: The bent stick and the stretched bands store the energy. When you let go, they spring back and fling the ball.
items.art: An empty box to draw in.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai argue about which is more elastic, a rubber band or a steel spring. Their teacher joins in.

views.says: The rubber band is more elastic. It stretches to twice its length and still comes back.
The steel spring is more elastic. It comes back almost perfectly every time, even after thousands of clicks in a pen. An old rubber band goes loose.
It depends what you mean. Do you mean how far it can stretch, or how perfectly it comes back?

items.ask: Which one do you think is more elastic? Give evidence from the tests in this unit. Then answer back from another side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence: a rubber band stretches much further, but a steel spring loses less and lasts longer, and old bands stay loose. It answers back fairly, and the best answers notice that 'elastic' can mean two different things.
items.why: Scientists say 'elastic' when a thing comes back fully. Rubber can stretch very far, but steel comes back more perfectly. Both friends have real evidence.

items.p: Three rubber bands each hold 20 coins. Band A stretches 1 cm. Band B stretches 4 cm. Band C stretches 8 cm. Put them in order from the stiffest to the least stiff.
items.a: order shown
items.why: A stiff band needs a bigger pull to stretch, so it stretches least with the same coins. Band A stretched least, so it is the stiffest.

items.p: Zoom deep into a steel spring and you find atoms in neat rows. Each atom is held to its neighbours by pulls called bonds. You stretch the spring a little. What do the bonds do?
opts: They stretch a tiny bit and pull the atoms back to their places
They break, and new ones grow
Nothing. Only the outside of the spring stretches
They turn into rubber
items.why: Each atom rests where the pulls from its neighbours balance. Pull the atoms a little apart, and the bonds pull them back, like tiny springs. Picking 'only the outside stretches' misses that every row of atoms stretches a little.

items.p: A girl bends a steel hairpin hard, and it stays bent. Her brother says, 'Some of the metal must have been squeezed out.' Is he right? Say what really happened to the atoms.
items.a: A strong answer says no, nothing was squeezed out. Every atom is still there. The bend went past the elastic limit, so rows of atoms slipped over each other and settled beside new neighbours. That is why the new shape stays.
items.why: Below the limit, bonds stretch and pull back. Past it, atoms move to new places. Nothing is lost, only moved.

items.p: Hang coins from a rubber band. Then blow warm air from a hair dryer on the band. The band gets a little shorter.
items.why: True, which surprises most people. Warmth makes the tangled chains inside rubber jiggle more. More jiggling shakes them back into a tangle harder, so the band pulls up. Most other things get a little longer when warm.

items.p: Rubber is made of long tangled chains, like a bowl of cooked noodles. What does stretching do to the chains?
opts: It pulls them straighter, and jiggling tangles them again when you let go
It cuts them into short pieces
It packs them into neat rows, like steel
It makes them melt
items.why: Stretching lines the chains up. The atoms in them jiggle all the time, and there are many more tangled ways than straight ways. So when you let go, they shake back into a tangle. Picking 'neat rows' is how steel is built, not rubber.

items.p: Robert Hooke, an English scientist, wanted to measure how a wire stretches. A short wire stretched too little to see. So he hung weights on a wire 6 to 12 metres long. Why did a long wire help?
items.a: A long wire has many more atoms in a row. Each little piece of wire stretches a tiny bit. All the tiny bits add up to a stretch big enough to measure.
items.why: This is the same reason two bands in a chain stretch twice as far as one.

items.p: Many people think heavy buildings cause earthquakes. Where do earthquakes really start?
opts: Many kilometres underground, where rock bends slowly for years and then suddenly slips
Under the heaviest buildings in a city
In the sky, when thunder shakes the ground
At the bottom of the sea only
items.why: The Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces that push on each other. The rock bends and stores energy, then slips in seconds. Harry Fielding Reid explained this in 1910. Buildings are far too small and too near the top to do it.

items.p: In the ruler earthquake, you press a ruler's free end down slowly. Then your finger slips off, and the ruler twangs. Which part is like the years before an earthquake? Which part is like the earthquake?
items.a: Pressing the ruler down slowly is like the years before: the rock bends and stores energy. The slip and the twang are like the earthquake: all the stored energy is let go at once, and everything shakes.
items.why: Rock is elastic, like the ruler. Under the Himalaya, rock is being squeezed by about 2 cm a year, storing energy for the next slip.
items.context: In the Bend or Snap? activity, you hold a ruler on a table and slowly press its free end down until it slips.

items.p: In 2015, an instrument in the United States called LIGO caught a gravitational wave, a ripple in space itself. LIGO has arms 4 kilometres long. How much did the wave stretch them?
opts: By less than the width of a tiny speck inside an atom
By about 1 metre
By about 1 centimetre
It snapped them
items.why: The stretch was less than a hundredth of the width of a proton. A proton is a speck inside an atom. That is why LIGO took decades to build. Picking 1 metre shows how hard it is to imagine something so small.

items.p: In Rubber Band Galaxies, you draw dots on a rubber strip, 1 cm apart, and stretch it. Which dot moves furthest away from the first dot, dot A?
opts: The dot furthest from A
The dot nearest to A
All the dots move the same amount
None of them move
items.why: Each piece of rubber between the dots stretches. The far dot has the most rubber between it and A, so it moves furthest. Astronomers see the same with galaxies: the furthest ones are moving away fastest. Picking 'all the same' misses that the stretches add up.

items.p: Scientists have measured space stretching. So they know what space is made of.
items.why: False. Measuring what something does is not the same as knowing what it is. We know space can stretch and ripple. Nobody yet knows what space is made of. Scientists have ideas, but no evidence for any of them yet.

items.p: Many people think stretchy things are weak. Spider silk is very stretchy, but weight for weight it is stronger than steel wire. Does that change the idea? Explain why stretching helps a web.
items.a: Yes. Spider silk shows a thing can be stretchy and strong at the same time. When a fly hits the web, the silk stretches and soaks up the push slowly, so it does not snap. A stiff thread would take the whole push at once and break.
items.why: Being able to stretch can make a material tougher, because it soaks up sudden pushes.

items.p: In the Bungee Doll challenge, a chain of 2 bands lets the doll drop 30 cm. 3 bands let it drop 40 cm. 4 bands let it drop 50 cm. Describe the pattern and predict 8 bands. Why might a real test not match exactly?
items.a: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 8 bands is 4 more than 4 bands, so 40 cm more: 50 + 40 = 90 cm. A real test might not match because bands are not all the same, and near their limit they stretch more than the pattern says.
items.why: The pattern goes up by the same amount each time, like the spring rule. Real bands can bend the line near their limit.

items.p: Long ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle had an idea about why things keep their shape. Scientists today explain it differently. A girl who did the pen spring test adds her own view.

views.who: Aristotle, a thinker in ancient Greece
views.says: Every thing has its own form. A spring keeps its shape because that shape belongs to what it is.
A spring's shape is just where the pulls between its atoms balance. Change the balance and the shape changes.
In my test, the spring came back to its own shape, until I pulled it too far. So it has a shape of its own, but only up to a limit.

items.ask: Which view fits best with what you saw? Use evidence from your own tests. Then answer back from another view.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses real evidence: the spring came back after gentle pulls, but stayed long after a hard pull, and a hairpin stays bent. It answers back fairly, for example that a spring does seem to 'want' its shape, or that the atoms explain exactly where the limit comes from.
items.why: Scientists explain springing back with balanced pulls between atoms. Some thinkers today still find Aristotle's idea useful. Kavya's view shows the evidence both sides must explain.

items.p: Robert Hooke wrote that every springy thing follows one rule: double the pull, double the stretch. Which result from a coin test shows the rule does not hold for big stretches?
opts: Near the end, each 5 coins stretched the band much more than before
Every 5 coins added exactly 1 cm
The band was 10 cm with no coins
The cup was made of paper
items.why: If the steps of stretch suddenly get bigger, the band no longer follows the rule. Later tests showed the rule works only for small stretches, below the elastic limit. Picking 'exactly 1 cm each time' is evidence for the rule, not against it.
items.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

items.p: Draw a model of the atoms in a spring, as balls joined by tiny springs. Then draw it again when the spring is stretched.
items.a: Two drawings. In the first, the balls are evenly spaced with short springs between them. In the second, the balls are a little further apart and every tiny spring is a little longer.
items.why: Stretching a spring stretches every bond between its atoms a tiny bit.

items.p: In 1986, rubber rings sealed the joints of the space shuttle Challenger's rockets. On a freezing morning, the cold rubber went stiff and sprang back too ____ to close the gap.
items.why: Cold rubber chains jiggle less, so they spring back slowly. The engineer Roger Boisjoly warned about this the night before. A seal failed, and the shuttle broke apart. Springing back on time can matter a great deal.

experiments.title: Coin by Coin: find the pattern, find the limit
experiments.context: This is the coin test. You hang a cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time, measuring the band each time. Then you pull a pen spring a little further each time, to find where it stops coming back.
experiments.question: When you add coins in equal handfuls, how does a rubber band's length change? And how far can a spring be pulled before it stops coming back?
experiments.predict: Before you add any coins, guess. Each time we add 5 coins, will the band grow by the same amount? By more and more? Or by less and less? Why do you think so? And if we pull a spring further and further, will it always come back? Why?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the number of coins. Use the same band, the same cup, the same kind of coins and the same ruler. Add exactly 5 coins each time. Wait until the cup stops bouncing, and read the ruler at eye level at the bottom of the band. For the pen spring, change only how far you pull it.

materials.item: a long, thin rubber band, about 10 cm long when it hangs empty. Thin bands stretch more, so they show the pattern best
a small paper cup, with a string handle threaded through two holes about 1 cm below the rim
40 coins of the same kind, such as 1-rupee coins. If you do not have that many, use level tablespoons of dry rice or dal, one spoonful in place of each 5 coins
a pencil, and two chairs to rest it on
a 30 cm ruler and some tape
the spring from an old clicky ballpoint pen

experiments.safety: Stand to the side, not over the cup, in case the band slips. A grown-up takes the spring out of the pen. Keep the spring's ends away from eyes.

schedule.what: Guess with a reason, add coins 5 at a time and measure, then pull a pen spring further each time until it stops coming back.

experiments.record: Fill in the coin table. Then make a second table for the pen spring. One column says how far you pulled it. The other says its length after you let go. Circle the first pull it did not come back from.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your band will be different. Look at the last column: that is where the pattern shows.

flow.do: 1. Stand two chairs back to back, about 10 cm apart. 2. Rest a pencil across the tops of their backs, and tape it down. 3. Loop the rubber band over the pencil. 4. Hook the cup's string handle on the bottom of the band. 5. Tape the top of the ruler to the pencil, right beside the band. It hangs straight down, with 0 at the top.
flow.say: We're going to hang coins on this band, 5 at a time. Each time, we'll measure how long the band is.
flow.kid: Put a pencil across two chairs. Hang the band on it. Hook the cup on the band. Tape the ruler beside it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coin test. You hang a cup from a rubber band, add coins 5 at a time, and measure the band.
flow.parent: Making the handle: poke two holes about 1 cm below the cup's rim with a pencil, thread a string through, and knot it. A paper clip bent into an S also works. The ruler hangs from the same pencil as the band, so it stays right beside it.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for a guess and a reason. 2. Write both at the top of the table. 3. Don't say whether it is right.
flow.say: Before we add anything, guess. Every time we add 5 coins, will the band grow by the same amount? By more and more? Or by less and less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will each 5 coins add the same stretch? More each time? Less each time? Say why.

ask.q: What do you think will happen, and why?
good: The same each time, because each 5 coins pull the same.
More and more, because the band gets thinner.
Less and less, because the band pulls back harder.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good guess. Don't hint. The coins will answer it. Some children pick 'more and more', because a long band looks weaker.

flow.do: 1. With the cup empty, read the ruler at the bottom of the band. 2. Write it next to 0 coins.
flow.say: Let's measure before any coins go in. Bring your eyes level with the bottom of the band. What does the ruler say?
flow.kid: Look at the bottom of the band, at eye level. Read the ruler. Write it next to 0 coins.
flow.parent: Looking from the side, at eye level, gives a true reading. Half centimetres are fine to write down.

flow.do: 1. Drop 5 coins gently into the cup. 2. Wait until it stops bouncing. 3. Measure and write the length. 4. Work out how much longer it is than last time, and write that too. 5. Repeat until there are 40 coins.
flow.say: Five more coins. Wait till it's still. What does the ruler say now? How much longer is that than last time?
flow.kid: Add 5 coins. Wait till it stops bouncing. Measure. How much longer than last time? Write both numbers.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table
cols: How much longer than last time (cm)

flow.parent: If each step is less than half a centimetre, the band is too thick or too short. Swap to a thinner, longer band. Or cut the band once, tie one end round the pencil and the other to the cup, so it hangs as one long strand. If the cup fills up before 40 coins, stop there. The step column is what matters.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to look only at the last column. 2. Ask what they notice before you say anything.
flow.say: Look at the last column, the steps. What do you notice about them? Was your guess right? What do you think is going on?
flow.kid: Look at your steps, in the last column. What do you notice? Was your guess right?

ask.q: What do you notice about the steps?
good: They are nearly all the same.
Each 5 coins added about 1 cm.
The last steps were a bit bigger.

check.q: Most of the steps were about the same size. What pattern does that show?
options: Equal handfuls of coins give equal steps of stretch
The band stretches only once, then stops
More coins make the band shorter
check.why: Equal handfuls gave equal steps. Scientists call this Hooke's law. Picking 'stretches only once' usually means only the first step was looked at. If your last steps were bigger, that is real too. Rubber follows the rule only roughly when it gets long.

flow.parent: Many bands give nearly equal steps, then slightly bigger steps near the end. Both are honest results. Write down what you really saw.

flow.do: 1. Take all the coins out. 2. Measure the band again.
flow.say: Now the coins are out. What do you think the ruler will say? Let's look.
flow.kid: Take the coins out. Measure the band. Is it back to its first length?

check.q: The coins are out, and the band is back to its first length. What does that show?
options: The band is elastic: it sprang back
check.why: It went back to its first length, so it is elastic. Picking 'broken' usually means stretching was thought to damage it. A small stretch does not.

flow.parent: A band that held 40 coins may be a few millimetres longer at first. Wait a minute and measure again. It usually shrinks back.

flow.do: 1. Unscrew an old clicky pen and take out the spring. 2. Lay it along the ruler and measure it. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Now a spring. We'll pull it a little further each time and let go. Will it always come back to this length? If not, when will it stop? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for the spring from a pen. Measure it. Will it always come back? Say why.

ask.q: Will the spring always come back? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because springs always come back.
No, if I pull too far it will stay long.
It will snap if I pull too hard.

flow.do: 1. Hold one end of the spring at 0 on the ruler. 2. Pull the other end 1 cm past its length, hold for 3 seconds, and let go. 3. Measure it and write it down. 4. Repeat, pulling to 2, 3, 5 and 7 cm past its first length. 5. At the end, pull it gently a little and let go.
flow.say: Pull it a little further. Let go. Measure. Did it come back? Now a little further. Where did it stop coming back?
flow.kid: Pull the spring a little further each time. Let go. Measure. When does it stop coming back?

check.q: The spring came back after small pulls. After a big pull, it stayed longer. What happened?
options: It was pulled past its elastic limit, so it changed inside
It slowly grows longer by itself
check.why: Past its elastic limit, the spring changed inside and took a new length. Picking 'grows longer by itself' misses that it changed only after the big pull. The small pulls left it the same. The next cards show what changed inside.

flow.parent: Most pen springs come back from small pulls. Many start to stay longer once pulled to about one and a half to two times their length. Yours may be different, so trust what you measure. At the end, a gentle pull still springs back, but now to its new length.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think now. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things in your own words. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think the spring stopped coming back?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: equal coins give equal stretches, but only up to a limit. What I saw: each 5 coins added about 1 cm, and the band came back. The pen spring came back from small pulls but stayed long after a big one. Why: maybe something inside it moved and couldn't move back. Don't correct the 'why' yet. The next cards test it.

experiments.title: Band Launch: does a longer stretch send a band further?
experiments.question: If you stretch a rubber band further before you let go, does it fly further?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a band pulled back to the 15 cm mark fly further than one pulled to the 10 cm mark, less far, or the same distance? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same band every time, and launch it from the same place at the same height. Hold the ruler flat and level each time. Change only how far you pull the band back. Try each pull 3 times, because one try can be a fluke. Then put the 3 distances in order and take the middle one.

materials.item: an ordinary small rubber band
a 30 cm ruler
about 4 metres of clear floor, such as the longest room or a corridor
a measuring tape, or count the floor tiles
a few coins, to mark where the band lands

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays for this. Everyone stands behind the person launching. Never aim at people, pets, faces or windows. Aim along the floor, away from everyone.

schedule.what: Launch a rubber band off a ruler with a short pull and a long pull, 3 times each, and measure how far it flies.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about which pull sent the band further.

setup.caption: 2. Pull the band back to a mark. Let go.
