flow.do: 1. Clear the floor of a corridor or a long room. 2. Stick a strip of tape on the floor at one end as the start line. 3. Everyone else stands behind the start line.
flow.say: We're going to launch a rubber band off the end of a ruler. Everyone stands behind me. We never aim at anyone.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to help. Clear the floor. Put tape down as a start line. Everyone stands behind you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Band Launch. You pull a rubber band back along a ruler, let go, and measure how far it flies.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the 10 cm and 15 cm marks on the ruler. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: First we'll pull the band back to the 10 cm mark. Then to the 15 cm mark. Which will fly further? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Pulled to 10 cm, or pulled to 15 cm. Which flies further? Say why.

ask.q: What do you think will happen, and why?
good: The 15 cm pull flies further, because the band is stretched more.
The same, because it is the same band.
The 10 cm pull, because a long stretch might wobble.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is a good guess. Don't hint. The band will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Sit behind the start line. Hook the band over the end of the ruler with 0 on it. 2. Hold the ruler flat and level, at chest height, with the 0 end pointing down the room. 3. Pull the band back along the ruler to the 10 cm mark. Let go. 4. Put a coin where the band stops. Measure from the start line. 5. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Pull it back to the 10 cm mark and let go. Where did it stop? Let's measure. Now two more tries the same way.
flow.kid: Hook the band on the 0 end of the ruler. Pull it back to 10 cm. Let go. Mark where it stops. Measure. Try 3 times.
flow.parent: Keep the ruler at the same height and level every time, or the test is not fair. If the band already reaches past the 10 cm mark without stretching, use a smaller band. If the band hits the far wall, use the 8 cm and 12 cm marks for every try instead. If you count floor tiles, write the number of tiles.

flow.do: 1. Now pull the band back to the 15 cm mark, the same way. 2. Let go, mark and measure. 3. Do it 3 times. 4. For each pull, put the 3 distances in order and circle the middle one. That is the middle value.
flow.say: Now pull it back to the 15 cm mark. Same height, same ruler. How far this time?
flow.kid: Now pull it back to 15 cm. Let go. Mark and measure. Try 3 times.

ask.q: Why did the longer pull send the band further?
good: It stored more energy.
It was stretched more, so it pulled back harder and faster.

check.q: The band pulled back to 15 cm flew further than the band pulled back to 10 cm. Why?
options: It stored more energy when it was stretched more
check.why: Stretching the band more stores more energy, and the band gives it back as speed. Picking 'lighter' or 'the ruler moved' means looking for another cause. In a fair test, only the pull changed.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things in your own words. What do you think now about stretching and flying? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: stretching a band more makes it fly further. What I saw: pulled to 10 cm, it went about 150 cm. Pulled to 15 cm, it went about 350 cm. Why: the more you stretch it, the more energy it stores, and it gives that energy back when it springs.

experiments.context: In this experiment you hook a rubber band over the 0 end of a ruler. You pull it back a little or a lot, let go, and measure how far it flies along the floor.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the band flew
example_chart.x: How far it was pulled back
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your band and floor will be different.

experiments.title: Find the Limit
experiments.question: When we stretch or bend different things, which spring back, which stay changed, and which snap?
experiments.predict: Before you test each thing, guess. Will it spring back, stay changed, or snap? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure each thing before you stretch it. Stretch each one to about twice its length, or bend it gently, then let go. Pull the pen spring only a little at first. Measure it again straight away. That way you compare each thing with itself.

materials.item: a rubber band
a strip cut from a thin plastic carry bag, about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide
an old pen spring
a rope of playdough or chapati dough, about 10 cm long
a stick of uncooked spaghetti, a thin dry twig or a used matchstick
a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the plastic strip. Bend the spaghetti away from your face. Throw away the plastic strip safely afterwards, so animals cannot eat it.

schedule.what: Measure, stretch and measure again: five things.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle the things that sprang back. Draw the pen spring before and after a very hard pull.

setup.art: Five things in a row on a table with a ruler: a rubber band, a plastic strip, a pen spring, a rope of dough and a stick of spaghetti.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the five things and measure each one.

setup.art: Two hands stretching the plastic strip to twice its length beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch each one to about twice its length.

setup.art: The plastic strip lying long and thin after being let go, beside the rubber band which is back to its first size.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Measure it again.

setup.art: Two hands gently bending a stick of uncooked spaghetti until it snaps.
setup.caption: 4. Bend the spaghetti gently. What happens?

flow.do: 1. Line up the five things. 2. Measure each one and write its length in the table. 3. Write your child's guess for each.
flow.say: Let's guess first. For each thing, will it spring back, stay stretched, or snap? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure each thing. Write the length. Then guess: spring back, stay, or snap?
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Limit. You stretch or bend five different things and see which spring back. Elastic things spring back. Every elastic thing has a limit.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the rubber band, plastic strip and dough to about twice their length. Pull the pen spring only a little. 2. Let go. 3. Measure each one again straight away. 4. Gently bend the spaghetti until it bends a little, then more.
flow.say: Stretch it to twice as long. Let go. Now measure. Is it the same as before?
flow.kid: Stretch each one to twice as long. Let go. Measure again. Bend the spaghetti gently. What happens?
flow.parent: Expect this. The rubber band springs back. The plastic strip stays long and thin. Playdough stays long. Chapati dough shrinks back a little, but stays longer than before. The pen spring springs back if pulled gently, but stays long if pulled hard. The spaghetti bends a tiny bit, then snaps.

flow.do: Pull the old pen spring very hard, far past twice its length. Let go and measure.
flow.say: Now let's pull the spring too far on purpose. What do you think it will do when we let go? Why?
flow.kid: Pull the old pen spring very hard. Let go. Did it come back? Measure it.

check.q: The pen spring was pulled very hard. Now it stays long and loose. Why?
options: It was pulled past its elastic limit
Springs always get longer over time
check.why: It went past its elastic limit, so rows of atoms slipped into new places. Picking 'never elastic' misses that it sprang back when pulled gently. Picking 'always get longer' mixes it up with wearing out slowly.

flow.think: The plastic strip and the spring both stayed long. What do you think changed inside them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things in your own words. Which things came back and which didn't? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think some stayed long?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: elastic things spring back, but only up to a limit. What I saw: the rubber band went back to 6 cm. The plastic strip went from 10 cm to 18 cm and stayed. The spaghetti snapped. The pen spring came back when I pulled it a little, but stayed long when I pulled it hard. Why: every elastic thing has a limit, and past it, it stays changed or breaks.

experiments.context: In this experiment you stretch or bend five things: a rubber band, a plastic strip, a pen spring, dough and spaghetti. You measure them before and after, to see which spring back, which stay changed and which snap.

experiments.title: The Bounce Test
experiments.question: Which ball bounces highest when dropped from the same height?
experiments.predict: Line up the balls. Put the one you think will bounce highest first, and the one you think will bounce lowest last. Why did you choose that order?
experiments.fair_test: Drop every ball from the same height, 1 metre, onto the same hard floor. Let go without pushing it down. Drop each ball 3 times and take the middle value.

materials.item: 3 or 4 different balls, for example a rubber ball, a tennis ball, a plastic ball and a sponge ball
a ball of chapati dough, the size of a lemon
a metre scale, or a 1-metre strip of paper taped to a wall and marked every 10 cm

experiments.safety: Do this on a clear, hard floor away from glass. Put the dough ball in the bin or the compost afterwards.

schedule.what: Drop each ball from 1 metre 3 times and measure the bounce. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each ball's middle value.

setup.art: A paper strip marked every 10 cm taped to a wall from the floor up to 1 metre, with balls lined up on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a 1-metre strip to the wall.

setup.art: A child holding a tennis ball level with the 1-metre mark, about to let go.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ball at the 1-metre mark. Let go.

setup.art: A grown-up crouching with eyes level with the strip, watching the top of the bounce.
setup.caption: 3. Watch how high the ball bounces back.

setup.art: A ball of dough flattened on the floor, not bouncing.
setup.caption: 4. Try the dough ball too.

flow.do: 1. Tape the strip to a wall, from the floor up. 2. Ask your child to put the balls in a line, highest bouncer first.
flow.say: Which ball do you think will bounce highest? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Put the balls in a line. Which will bounce highest? Put that one first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bounce Test. You drop different balls from 1 metre and measure how high each one bounces back.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It's made of rubber.
It feels springy.

flow.do: 1. Hold a ball with its bottom at the 1-metre mark. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. The other person watches the strip at eye level and calls out how high the bottom of the ball gets. 4. Do each ball 3 times.
flow.say: Just open your fingers. Don't throw it. Watch the strip. How high did it come back up?
flow.kid: Hold the ball at the top mark. Just let go. Watch how high it comes back. Try each ball 3 times.
flow.parent: The top of a bounce is fast. Do a test drop first, then watch only the right part of the strip. A phone video in slow motion helps too.

flow.do: Drop the dough ball from 1 metre too.
flow.say: Now the dough. Do you think it will bounce? Why? Let's see.
flow.kid: Drop the dough ball. Does it bounce? What shape is it now?

check.q: The dough ball did not bounce. It went flat. Why?
options: Dough is hardly elastic, so it does not spring back
It was dropped from too low
check.why: A bounce needs a squash and a spring back. Dough squashes but stays squashed. Picking 'too low' or 'too light' means looking for another cause. A rubber ball from the same height still bounces.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each ball. A taller bar means a higher bounce.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each ball. Make it as tall as its middle bounce. Which ball is best?

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things in your own words. Which ball is the most elastic? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think the dough did not bounce?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think now. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rubber ball is the most elastic, so it bounces highest. What I saw: from 1 metre it bounced back 80 cm, but the dough ball did not bounce at all. Why: a ball bounces by squashing and springing back. Dough squashes but does not spring back. No ball comes all the way back, because some energy turns into heat and sound.

experiments.context: This is the Bounce Test. You drop different balls from 1 metre onto a hard floor and measure how high each one bounces back. A bounce is a squash and a spring back.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each ball bounced back from 1 metre
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your balls will be different.

activities.title: Spring Hunt

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil, to list what you find

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Only bend low, thin, living branches gently, and let them go slowly.

schedule.what: Hunt for springs and elastic things indoors, then on a short walk.

activities.record: Find 12 springs or elastic things. Write each one down. Next to it, write its job: to stretch, to squash, to bend or to bounce.

setup.art: A child opening a clothes peg and looking at its twisty spring.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt indoors: pens, pegs, beds, hair bands.

setup.art: A child gently bending a low green branch and watching it spring back.
setup.caption: 2. Outdoors: find a springy branch and bend it gently.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a list of springy things and little drawings beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Write each find and its job.

flow.do: Explain the hunt to your child, and give them the paper and pencil.
flow.say: We're spring detectives. Springs and elastic things are hiding all over our home. Let's find 12.
flow.kid: You are a spring detective! Find 12 springs or elastic things. Elastic means it springs back.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spring Hunt. Elastic things change shape when pushed or pulled, and spring back when you let go.

flow.do: 1. Hunt around the home. 2. Look at pens, clothes pegs, the stapler, the mattress and the sofa. 3. Look at hair bands, pyjama elastic, a cycle seat and a woven cot. 4. If you go outside with a grown-up, find a low green branch.
flow.say: For each one, what is its job? Does it stretch, squash, bend or bounce? What would happen if it were not elastic?
flow.kid: For each find, say its job. Does it stretch, squash, bend or bounce? Write it down.
flow.parent: Good finds include the squash spring in a clicky pen and the twisty spring in a clothes peg. Look for stretch springs in a spring balance or a trampoline. The elastic in socks, a hair band and the springs in a cycle seat count too. Outdoors, a low green branch bends and springs back.

flow.do: Ask each person to share their best find.
flow.say: Which find surprised you most? Which one would be a disaster if it were not elastic?
flow.kid: Which find surprised you most? Draw it.
flow.think: Who designed these springs? Why did they choose a spring, and not something stiff?

activities.context: This is a hunt around your home and street for springs and elastic things. You find out what job each one does.

activities.title: Two in a Row, Two Side by Side
activities.context: In this activity you hang the same coins from one rubber band, from two bands joined in a chain, and from two bands side by side. You find out why a long spring stretches more and a thick one less.

materials.item: 3 rubber bands of the same size
the coin test cup with its string handle, and 20 coins of the same kind
a pencil across two chairs, and a 30 cm ruler

activities.safety: Stand to the side, not over the cup, in case a band slips.

schedule.what: Guess, then hang 20 coins from one band, two bands in a chain and two bands side by side.

activities.record: Write three stretches: one band, two in a chain, two side by side. A stretch is the length with coins take away the length without coins.

setup.art: One rubber band hanging from a pencil holding a cup of coins, a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 1. One band, 20 coins. Measure the stretch.

setup.art: Two rubber bands joined in a chain, one looped through the other, holding the same cup.
setup.caption: 2. Two bands in a chain. Same 20 coins.

setup.art: Two rubber bands hanging side by side from the pencil, the cup hooked on both of them.
setup.caption: 3. Two bands side by side. Same 20 coins.

flow.do: 1. Hang one band from the pencil and measure it with the empty cup. 2. Add 20 coins and measure again. 3. Take away the first number from the second to get the stretch.
flow.say: First, one band and 20 coins. How long is it empty? How long with the coins? So how much did it stretch?
flow.kid: Hang one band. Measure it empty. Add 20 coins. Measure again. How much did it stretch?
flow.context: This is the first step of Two in a Row, Two Side by Side. You compare one band, two bands in a chain and two bands side by side.

flow.do: Ask for two guesses, each with a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: Now we'll join two bands in a chain and hang the same 20 coins. Will the chain stretch as much as one band, twice as much, or half as much? Why? And what about two bands side by side?
flow.kid: Guess. Two bands in a chain: same stretch, twice, or half? Two side by side? Say why.

ask.q: What will each one do, and why?
good: The chain stretches twice as much, because each band stretches.
Side by side stretches half, because they share the coins.
The same, because it's the same coins.

flow.do: 1. Loop a second band through the first, so they hang in a chain. 2. Measure the empty chain with the cup. 3. Add the 20 coins and measure again. 4. Work out the stretch.
flow.say: Here's the chain. Measure it empty, then with the coins. How much did it stretch this time?
flow.kid: Hang two bands in a chain. Measure empty. Add 20 coins. Measure. Work out the stretch.
flow.parent: Measure the empty chain first, because two bands are longer to start with. Only the stretch is compared.

flow.do: 1. Hang two bands side by side over the pencil. 2. Hook the cup's handle through both. 3. Measure empty, then with 20 coins.
flow.say: Now side by side. Both bands hold the cup. How much did they stretch?
flow.kid: Hang two bands side by side. Hook the cup on both. Measure empty, then with coins.

flow.do: Put the three stretches next to each other and ask what your child notices.
flow.say: Look at the three stretches. What do you notice? Why do you think the chain stretched more, and the pair side by side less?
flow.kid: Look at your three stretches. What do you notice? Why do you think so?

check.q: Two bands in a chain stretched about twice as far as one band. Why?
options: Each band in the chain holds all 20 coins, so each stretches as much as one band alone
The chain is heavier, so the coins pull harder
check.why: Every band in the chain carries the whole pull, so their stretches add up. Picking 'heavier' is a fair guess, but a rubber band weighs far less than 20 coins. Picking 'weaker' misses that side by side, the same bands stretched less.

flow.parent: Made-up example: one band stretched 4 cm, the chain 8 cm, and the pair side by side 2 cm. Your numbers will differ, but the chain is usually about double and the pair about half. If one band stretches less than 1 cm, use 40 coins instead of 20.
flow.think: A long wire is like many tiny springs in a row. What could the tiny springs be?

activities.title: The Springs in My Body

materials.item: some open floor space and a soft mat

activities.safety: Jump on a soft mat or grass. Stop if anything hurts.

schedule.what: Feel your tendons, skin and pulse working like springs.

activities.record: Draw yourself jumping. Mark three springy parts of your body.

setup.art: A child jumping with stiff straight legs beside a child jumping with bent, bouncy legs.
setup.caption: 1. Jump with stiff legs, then with bendy legs.

setup.art: A child pinching the skin on the back of their hand and letting go.
setup.caption: 2. Pinch the skin on your hand. Let go.

setup.art: A child's fingers feeling the thick cord at the back of their ankle.
setup.caption: 3. Find your Achilles tendon at the back of your ankle.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to do 5 small jumps with stiff, straight knees. 2. Then 5 jumps with bendy, springy knees.
flow.say: Jump with stiff legs. Now jump with bendy legs. Which is easier? Which is higher?
flow.kid: Jump 5 times with stiff legs. Now 5 times with bendy knees. Which feels better?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Springs in My Body. Your body is full of parts that stretch and spring back, like springs.

flow.do: 1. Find the thick cord at the back of your ankle. 2. Stand on tiptoe and feel it go tight.
flow.say: Find the thick cord at the back of your ankle. Stand on tiptoe, then come down. What does the cord do? What do you think its job is when you jump?
flow.kid: Feel the back of your ankle. That cord is a tendon. Stand on tiptoe. Feel it go tight!

ask.q: Which animals use big springy tendons to hop?
good: Kangaroos.
Rabbits.

flow.parent: After your child has guessed, give the name. This is the Achilles tendon. It stretches when you land and springs back as you push off, giving back most of the energy.

flow.do: 1. Pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it. 2. Then press two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist and feel your pulse.
flow.say: Pinch the skin on the back of your hand and let go. Watch it closely. Why do you think it goes back? Now feel the beat in your wrist. What could be stretching there?
flow.kid: Pinch your skin. Let go. What does it do? Now feel your wrist. What could be stretching there?

check.q: Your skin springs back after a pinch. That means skin is…
check.why: Skin springs back, so it is elastic. Picking 'brittle' means skin was pictured snapping, which it does not. Picking 'stays changed' is what happens to dough, not skin.

flow.parent: After your child answers: skin springs back because of a stretchy material called elastin. The beat is a blood vessel stretching each time the heart squeezes, then springing back.

flow.do: Tell your child about the flea.
flow.say: A flea jumps much faster than their muscles can move. How do you think they do it? Think of a catapult.
flow.kid: A flea jumps faster than their muscles can move. How? Think of a catapult.
flow.think: If you were an animal designer, where would you put springs?
flow.parent: After their guess: a flea's muscles slowly squash a pad of a rubbery stuff called resilin, and lock it. Then the flea lets go all at once, like a catapult.

activities.context: In this activity you find the springs in your own body: your tendons, your skin and the blood vessel that beats in your wrist.

activities.title: Rubber Band Galaxies

materials.item: a wide rubber band, cut once to make a strip, or a strip of wide elastic
a felt pen and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the band. Stretch it gently.

schedule.what: Draw galaxies on a band, stretch it and measure how they move apart.

activities.record: Write how far apart the dots were before and after stretching. Which dots moved apart the most?

setup.art: A wide rubber strip lying on a table with five dots drawn on it, 1 cm apart, labelled A to E.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 5 dots on the strip, 1 cm apart.

setup.art: Two hands stretching the strip to twice its length beside a ruler, the dots now 2 cm apart.
setup.caption: 2. Stretch it to twice as long.

setup.art: A ruler measuring from dot A to dot E on the stretched strip.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far each dot moved from dot A.

flow.do: 1. Lay the strip flat. 2. Draw 5 dots, 1 cm apart. Label them A, B, C, D and E.
flow.say: Each dot is a galaxy, a giant family of stars. Dot A is our galaxy, the Milky Way.
flow.kid: Draw 5 dots, 1 cm apart. Each dot is a galaxy. Dot A is our home.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rubber Band Galaxies. The universe is slowly stretching. A rubber strip with dots on it shows how.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the strip to twice its length and hold it. 2. Measure from dot A to each other dot.
flow.say: Stretch it. Now how far is B from A? And E from A? Which dot moved further?
flow.kid: Stretch the strip to double. Measure from A to each dot. Which one moved furthest?

ask.q: Which dot moved away from A the most?
good: E, the furthest one.
The far ones moved more.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far each dot is from dot A

flow.do: 1. Ask your child why the far dot moved most, and wait for an answer. 2. Then talk about the real universe.
flow.say: No one pushed any dot. So why did dot E end up furthest away? Take your time. Astronomers see far galaxies moving away from us faster than near ones. What do you think is stretching?
flow.kid: No one pushed any dot. So why did dot E move furthest? Think, then tell someone.

check.q: On the stretched strip, which dot moved furthest from dot A?
check.why: The furthest dot moved most, because there is more stretching rubber between it and dot A. Picking 'nearest' or 'all the same' means the dots were pictured moving by themselves. It is the rubber between them that stretches.

flow.think: If you lived on dot C, would you think you were at the centre? Is anyone at the centre?
flow.parent: After your child answers, explain. The rubber between the dots stretched, and dot E has the most rubber between it and dot A. Astronomers think the space between galaxies is stretching in a similar way. From any dot, all the others seem to move away, so there is no centre.

activities.context: In this activity you draw dots on a rubber strip and stretch it. It shows how the universe is stretching, with galaxies getting further apart.

activities.title: Rubber Band Orchestra

materials.item: an empty tissue box or an open shoe box
4 rubber bands of different thicknesses
2 pencils

activities.safety: Pluck gently. Keep faces away from tight bands.

schedule.what: Make a rubber band box guitar and test how stretch and thickness change the note.

activities.record: Write which band makes the highest note and which makes the lowest. Write what happens when you stretch a band tighter.

setup.art: An open shoe box with four rubber bands of different thicknesses stretched round it, two pencils under the bands as bridges.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch 4 bands round a box. Slide 2 pencils under them.

setup.art: A finger plucking one rubber band, which blurs as it vibrates.
setup.caption: 2. Pluck each band. Listen.

setup.art: A hand pulling one band tighter round the box while another hand plucks it.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch one band tighter. Pluck again.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the four bands round the box, over the opening. 2. Slide a pencil under the bands at each end.
flow.say: Let's build a guitar from springs. Each band is a spring that we will pluck.
flow.kid: Put 4 bands round the box. Slide a pencil under them at each end. Now you have a guitar!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Orchestra, one of the DeepKids ideas. A plucked rubber band springs back and forth very fast. That makes a sound.

flow.do: 1. Pluck each band and listen. 2. Watch how it blurs.
flow.say: Pluck each band and watch it closely. What is the band doing? Which band makes the lowest note? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pluck each band. Watch it blur. What is the band doing?

ask.q: Which band makes the lowest note?
good: The thickest one.
The loose one.

flow.parent: After they answer: the band springs back past its middle, then back again, very fast. That shaking is called vibrating, and it makes the sound.

flow.do: Pull one band tighter round the box, and pluck it again.
flow.say: Before you pluck it, guess. If we stretch this band tighter, will the note go higher or lower? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stretch one band tighter. Pluck it. Higher note or lower?

check.q: You stretch a rubber band tighter and pluck it. What happens to the note?
check.why: A tighter band pulls back harder and shakes faster, which makes a higher note. Picking 'lower' often comes from thinking a longer stretch must sound deeper. Listen again to check.

flow.parent: After they test it: a tighter band pulls back harder, so it shakes faster. Faster shaking makes a higher note.

flow.do: Talk about Indian instruments and C. V. Raman.
flow.say: A veena, a sitar and a tabla all use stretched strings or stretched skins. In 1920, the Indian scientist C. V. Raman worked out why Indian drums like the tabla and mridangam sound so musical. The secret is the black patch on the drum skin.
flow.kid: A veena and a tabla use stretched strings and skins. C. V. Raman, an Indian scientist, found out why the drums sound so musical.
flow.think: Which instruments in your home or temple use something stretched?

activities.context: In this activity you build a box guitar from rubber bands. You find out how stretching a band tighter changes its note.

activities.title: Bend or Snap? Twigs and the Ruler Earthquake

materials.item: a fresh green twig and a dry dead twig of about the same thickness. A twig from a potted plant works. If you have no dry twig, use a used matchstick
a plastic ruler

activities.safety: Snap twigs pointing away from faces. Do not bend the ruler until it breaks. Pick twigs that have already fallen, or ask before taking a small piece.

schedule.what: Bend a green and a dry twig. Make a ruler 'earthquake'.

activities.record: Draw the green twig and the dry twig after bending. Write which one sprang back.

setup.art: Two hands bending a green twig into a curve, and beside it a dry twig snapping.
setup.caption: 1. Bend a green twig and a dry twig.

setup.art: A plastic ruler held flat on a table with one end hanging over the edge, a finger pressing the end down.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a ruler on the table. Press the free end down slowly.

setup.art: The ruler end slipping off the finger and springing up with a twang, shaking lines around it.
setup.caption: 3. Let your finger slip off. Twang! That is an earthquake.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess and a reason. 2. Gently bend the green twig, then let go. 3. Gently bend the dry twig the same amount.
flow.say: Before we bend them, guess. Which twig will spring back, and which will snap? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Bend the green twig. Let go. Now bend the dry twig. Which one snapped?
flow.context: This is the first step of Bend or Snap. You compare a living twig and a dead one. Then you use a ruler to show how earthquakes happen.

flow.do: 1. Hold a plastic ruler flat on a table with about half of it over the edge. 2. Press the free end down slowly with one finger. 3. Keep pressing until it slips off your finger.
flow.say: Press the end down slowly, and keep going until it slips off your finger. What do you feel and hear when it slips? Where do you think that twang came from?
flow.kid: Hold the ruler on the table. Press the end down slowly. Keep going until it slips. Twang!

ask.q: What happened when the ruler slipped?
good: It sprang back and shook.
It made a twang and wobbled.

flow.parent: After your child answers: the ruler stored energy as it bent. It let the energy go all at once, as shaking and sound. Rock underground bends slowly for years in the same way. When it slips, the shaking is an earthquake.

flow.do: Bend the green twig again, a little more each time. Each time, check if it springs all the way back.
flow.say: Let's bend our green twig a little more each time. Will it always come all the way back? What do you expect to see?
flow.kid: Bend the green twig a bit more each time. Does it still come all the way back?

check.q: A branch bends under a swing. When you get off, it stays a little bent. What does that warn you?
options: It has passed its elastic limit and may break soon
It is fine, because it is still bending
check.why: A branch that stays bent has passed its elastic limit, so it may break soon. Picking 'it is fine' is a common idea, because bending itself is safe. The warning is when it stops coming back. Picking 'stronger' is the opposite of what happens.

flow.think: Is bending a kind of strength?

activities.context: In this activity you bend a green twig and a dry twig to see which springs back. You bend a ruler until it slips, to feel how an earthquake happens. Then you watch a twig for the warning sign of the elastic limit.

projects.title: The Rubber Band Car

materials.item: a small empty plastic bottle or a juice carton
4 bottle caps for wheels
2 wooden skewers or thin sticks for axles, and 2 drinking straws
2 or 3 rubber bands
tape, and a paper clip
a measuring tape or a long strip of paper marked every 10 cm

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the caps, using a hot skewer or a sharp tool. Snip the sharp tips off skewers.

schedule.what: Build the car body and the wheels.
Add the rubber band motor. Test it with 5, 10 and 15 winds.
Improve the car and hold a race.

projects.record: Write how far the car went with 5, 10 and 15 winds. Draw your car and label where the energy is stored.

setup.art: A plastic bottle lying on its side with two straws taped across its underside, a skewer through each straw, and bottle caps pushed on the ends as wheels.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two straws under the bottle. Push skewers through. Add cap wheels.

setup.art: A rubber band hooked to a paper clip at the front of the bottle, its other end looped round the back axle.
setup.caption: 2. Hook a rubber band from the front to the back axle.

setup.art: A child turning the back wheels backwards so the band winds round the axle.
setup.caption: 3. Wind the back wheels backwards. The band twists round the axle.

setup.art: The car rolling along the floor beside a paper strip marked every 10 cm.
setup.caption: 4. Let go and measure how far it goes.

flow.do: 1. Tape two straws across the bottom of the bottle, one near each end. 2. Push a skewer through each straw. 3. A grown-up makes a hole in the middle of each cap. 4. Push a cap onto each end of each skewer. The hole must be tight, so the cap turns with the skewer. If it is loose, fix it with tape or a drop of glue.
flow.say: We're building a car that runs on a rubber band. First, the body and the wheels.
flow.kid: Tape two straws under the bottle. Push a stick through each one. A grown-up makes holes in the caps. Push on the wheels.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber Band Car project. You build a little car whose motor is a twisted rubber band.

flow.do: 1. Check that the wheels turn freely. 2. If they rub on the bottle, slide the straws further out. 3. Roll the car gently to test it.
flow.say: A good car rolls easily. Spin each wheel. Does it rub anywhere? What do you think rubbing would do to the car?
flow.kid: Spin each wheel. Does it turn easily? If it rubs, move the straw. Roll the car.
flow.parent: Wheels that wobble or rub are the most common problem. A drop of oil or soap on the skewer can help.

flow.do: 1. Hook one end of a rubber band on a paper clip taped to the front of the bottle. 2. Loop the other end round the back axle and tape it once to the axle.
flow.say: Now the motor. When we wind the wheels backwards, what do you think happens to the band? Where will the car get its push from?
flow.kid: Hook a band to the front. Loop it round the back axle. Tape it on. That is the motor!
flow.wait: Leave the car for the next day's tests.

flow.do: 1. Turn the back wheels backwards 5 times. 2. Put the car down at the start of the paper strip and let go. 3. Measure how far it goes. 4. Repeat with 10 winds and 15 winds.
flow.say: Five winds. Let go! How far? Now ten. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Wind the back wheels backwards 5 times. Let go. Measure. Now try 10 winds, then 15.

check.q: The car went further with 15 winds than with 5 winds. Why?
options: The band stored more energy when wound more
check.why: More winds twist the band more, so it stores more energy. Picking 'lighter' or 'smoother floor' means looking for another cause. Only the winds changed.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far the rubber band car went
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your car will be different.

flow.do: 1. Choose one thing to improve: a second band, bigger wheels, or less rubbing. 2. Change only that one thing and test again.
flow.say: Engineers change one thing at a time. Then they know what made the difference. What will you change?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Maybe two bands, or bigger wheels. Test it again. Better or worse?
flow.parent: Too many winds can snap the band or make the wheels spin and skid. That is the elastic limit again.

flow.do: Hold a race with family or friends. Ask your child to explain how the car works.
flow.say: Tell everyone where the energy comes from, and where it is stored.
flow.kid: Race your car! Then explain it. Where is the energy stored?
flow.think: Your arm wound the band. Where did your arm get the energy from?

projects.context: In this 3-day project, you build a little car from a bottle and bottle caps. Its motor is a rubber band that you twist round the back axle. The twisted band stores energy and turns the wheels.

challenges.title: The Catapult Challenge
challenges.problem: Build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands. It must land a paper ball in a bowl 1 metre away.
constraints: Use only ice-cream sticks, rubber bands, a plastic spoon or bottle cap, and tape.
Never aim at people, animals or windows.
materials: a plastic spoon or bottle cap
general: Stack 6 sticks and tie them with bands at both ends. Put this stack between 2 more sticks tied together at one end. The top stick becomes the arm.
Tape a bottle cap or spoon to the end of the arm to hold the paper ball.
Pull the arm down further to fire further. More bend stores more energy.
creative: Change the stack height. A taller stack lets the arm bend further.
Use two rubber bands at the front to make a stiffer spring.
Mark lines on the arm and test how far each pull-back fires. Then you can aim like a scientist, not by guessing.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own design. Draw it, build it, and test it. Can you hit the bowl 3 times in a row?

setup.caption: 1. Tie a stack of 6 sticks.

setup.art: Two sticks tied together at one end, with the stack pushed between them, making a V shape.
setup.caption: 2. Push the stack between two sticks tied at one end.

setup.caption: 3. Tape on a cap. Load a paper ball. Press down and let go.

setup.caption: 4. Aim for the bowl 1 metre away.

flow.do: Build the basic catapult with your child, using the usual design.
flow.say: Let's build the usual catapult first. Look at the arm when it's done. What do you think will fling the ball, and why?
flow.kid: Build the catapult. Tie the stack. Push it between two sticks. Tape on the cap.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Catapult Challenge. You build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands, and aim at a bowl. Building a catapult is one of the DeepKids ideas.
flow.parent: Building it is the slowest part. If the bands keep slipping, wrap them twice.

flow.do: 1. Press the arm down a little and fire. 2. Then press it down a lot. 3. Measure how far each one goes.
flow.say: Small press, big press. Which do you think will go further? Why? Let's measure both.
flow.kid: Press the arm down a little. Fire. Now press a lot. Fire. Measure both.

check.q: Pressing the catapult arm down further makes the paper ball go…
options: Further, because more energy is stored
Less far, because the arm bends too much
check.why: Pressing further bends the arm more and stores more energy, so the ball goes further. Picking 'bends too much' is right only past the stick's limit, when it stays bent or snaps.

flow.do: Mark lines on the arm. Fire from each line and measure. Then use your marks to aim for the bowl.
flow.say: Now mark lines on the arm and fire from each one. Which line do you think will reach 1 metre? Why? Let's measure and see.
flow.kid: Mark lines on the arm. Fire from each one. Which line reaches the bowl?

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas together, then invent something new.
flow.say: People have used bent wood and twisted ropes to throw things for thousands of years. What can you invent?
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Now invent your own change. Can you hit the bowl 3 times?
flow.think: A bow, a catapult and a trampoline all store energy by bending. What else does?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a catapult from ice-cream sticks and rubber bands. You aim a paper ball into a bowl 1 metre away.

challenges.title: Bungee Doll
challenges.problem: A small doll or soft toy goes on a 'bungee jump' from a table. It hangs from a chain of rubber bands. Make it fall as close to the floor as you can, without its head touching.
constraints: Use only rubber bands, all the same size.
You must predict how many bands to use before the final jump.
The doll must not touch the floor.
materials: a small doll or soft toy
15 to 20 rubber bands of the same size
general: Test with 2, 3 and 4 bands. Measure how far the doll falls each time.
Find how much further each extra band lets it fall.
Measure the table height and work out how many bands fit.
creative: Draw a line graph of bands and fall distance. Use the line to predict.
Use a thicker band at the top to make the chain stiffer.
Real bungee cords are bundles of many thin rubber strands, which work like many bands side by side.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your prediction. How many bands? Test it once. How close did you get?

setup.caption: 1. Loop rubber bands into a chain.

setup.art: A doll tied by its feet to the end of a short chain of bands, the other end held at a table edge.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the doll's feet to the chain. Hold the top at the table edge.

setup.art: The doll dropping down below the table, the chain stretched, with a ruler standing on the floor beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Drop the doll. Measure how far down it gets.

setup.caption: 4. Predict the number of bands for the closest safe jump.

flow.do: 1. Make a chain of 2 rubber bands. 2. Tie it round the doll's feet. 3. Hold the top end at the table edge, with the doll at the edge too.
flow.say: This doll is going bungee jumping. We'll find out how many bands she needs to come close to the floor, but not touch it.
flow.kid: Loop 2 bands together. Tie them to the doll's feet. Hold the top at the table edge.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bungee Doll. A doll hangs from a chain of rubber bands and drops off a table. You must predict how many bands to use.

flow.do: 1. Drop the doll and watch its lowest point. 2. Measure from the table top to the doll's head at its lowest point. 3. Repeat with 3 and 4 bands. 4. Write the results in a table.
flow.say: Watch the lowest point, not where it ends up. How much further did each extra band let it fall?
flow.kid: Drop the doll. Watch its lowest point. Measure it. Now try 3 bands, then 4. Write them down.
flow.parent: A phone video helps you see the lowest point. Each extra band usually adds about the same extra distance.

chart.title: Made-up example: how far the doll fell
cols: Lowest point below the table top (cm)

flow.do: 1. Measure the table height. 2. Work out how many bands should bring the doll close to the floor. 3. Make your prediction and test it.
flow.say: Look at your table. How much further did each extra band let the doll fall? How tall is our table? So how many bands can we use, and why?
flow.kid: Measure the table. How much does each band add? How many bands do you need? Test it!

check.q: 2 bands: 30 cm. 3 bands: 40 cm. 4 bands: 50 cm. How far for 6 bands?
check.why: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 4 bands is 50 cm, so 6 bands is 2 more bands: 50 + 20 = 70 cm. Picking 60 cm usually means counting 10 cm for each band from zero. Picking 100 cm doubles 50, but the pattern adds, it does not double.

flow.do: Compare your prediction with what happened, then read the ideas together.
flow.say: How close did you get? What would you change?
flow.kid: How close did you get? What would you change next time?
flow.think: Real bungee jumpers trust their lives to this kind of maths. Why must engineers test cords many times?

challenges.context: This is a prediction challenge. A doll on a chain of rubber bands drops from a table. You test, find the pattern, and predict how many bands to use so it gets close to the floor without touching.

quiz.p: You hold a steel ruler flat on a table, bend its free end down a little and let go. It flicks straight again. What does this show?
opts: A hard thing can still be elastic
Only soft things are elastic
The ruler has stayed changed
quiz.why: The steel ruler is hard, but it went back to its old shape, so it is elastic. Elastic means springing back, not being soft. 'Stayed changed' is the opposite of what the ruler did.

quiz.p: You squeeze a sponge and let go. It puffs back up. What word fits the sponge?
opts: Elastic
Brittle
Stays changed
quiz.why: It changed shape and went back, so it is elastic. Brittle things snap. 'Stays changed' is the opposite of what the sponge did.

quiz.p: In the coin stretch test, what should stay the same every time you add coins?
opts: The rubber band, the cup and how you read the ruler
Nothing. Change everything
The number of coins
quiz.why: Only the number of coins should change. Then you know the coins caused the stretch. Picking 'the number of coins' gets it backwards: that is the one thing you change.
quiz.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

quiz.p: A band is 10 cm long with no coins. Each 5 coins make it 1 cm longer. How many coins make it 13 cm long?
opts: 15 coins
13 coins
3 coins
quiz.why: 13 cm is 3 cm longer than 10 cm. Each 1 cm needs 5 coins. 3 times 5 is 15 coins. Picking 3 coins counts the centimetres, not the coins.
quiz.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

quiz.p: A rubber band held 30 coins. You take the coins off, and now the band is 2 cm longer than before. What does this tell you?
opts: The coins pulled it past its elastic limit
The band has become more elastic
The coins added some rubber to it
quiz.why: An elastic band goes all the way back. This one stayed longer, so the coins pulled it past its elastic limit. It is now less elastic, not more.

quiz.p: What is a warning sign that something is near its elastic limit?
opts: It no longer goes all the way back to its old shape
It springs back very quickly
It feels cold
quiz.why: When a thing stays a little stretched or bent, it is near its limit and may soon break. This is what Ammu saw in the swing branch in the story.

quiz.p: Pulling a catapult back further makes the paper ball fly further. Why?
opts: A bigger stretch stores more energy
The ball gets lighter
The air pushes the ball harder
quiz.why: More stretch stores more energy, up to the elastic limit. Letting go turns that energy into movement.

quiz.p: Before you let go of a wound-up toy, where is the energy kept?
opts: In its tightly coiled spring
In its wheels
In the air around it
quiz.why: Winding coils the spring tighter and stores energy in it. As the spring unwinds, it turns the wheels.

quiz.p: What job does the spring in a clothes peg do?
opts: It snaps the jaws shut so the peg grips
It makes the peg lighter
It lets the peg stretch longer
quiz.why: When you squeeze the peg, you bend its spring. Let go, and the spring springs back and closes the jaws.

quiz.p: When you land from a jump, which part of you stretches and then springs back to help the next jump?
opts: The tendon at the back of your ankle
Your eyebrows
Your teeth
quiz.why: This tendon is called the Achilles tendon. It stretches as you land and springs back as you push off, so you use less effort.

quiz.p: A steel spring springs back even when it is upside down or lying sideways. What does that tell us?
opts: Pulls between its atoms bring it back, not gravity
Gravity pulls it back every time
There is air trapped inside it
quiz.why: Gravity only pulls down, so it cannot pull a spring back sideways. The bonds between atoms pull each atom back to its resting place, whichever way the spring faces.

quiz.p: Three of the same rubber bands are joined in a chain. The same coins hang from it. Compared with one band, about how far does the chain stretch?
opts: About three times as far
About a third as far
The same
quiz.why: Each band in the chain carries all the coins, so each stretches as much as one band alone. Three stretches add up. Picking 'a third' mixes it up with bands side by side, which share the pull.

quiz.p: Why does a spring that was pulled past its elastic limit stay long?
opts: Rows of its atoms slipped into new places and stay there
Some of its atoms fell out
It got colder and shrank back the wrong way
quiz.why: Past the limit, rows of atoms slip and settle beside new neighbours. Every atom is still there, just in a new place, so the new shape stays.

quiz.p: For hundreds of years before an earthquake, what is the rock deep underground doing?
opts: Slowly bending and storing energy
Slowly melting
Staying perfectly still
quiz.why: Giant pieces of the Earth push on each other, so the rock bends slowly, like a pressed ruler. Then it slips all at once, and the ground shakes.

quiz.p: What does a gravitational wave do as it passes?
opts: It stretches and squeezes space itself, by a tiny amount
It makes waves on the sea
It is a beam of light
quiz.why: Gravitational waves are ripples in space. LIGO measured one in 2015. Picking 'the sea' mixes them up with ocean waves.

quiz.p: After a giant earthquake in Chile in 1960, what did instruments find the whole Earth doing for days?
opts: Vibrating slowly, like a bell after it is struck
Spinning backwards
Getting bigger
quiz.why: Rock is elastic, so the whole planet rang like a bell. The shaking travelled through it as waves.

applications: Hanging spring balances, luggage scales and forcemeters measure weight by how far a spring stretches.
Clicky pens, staplers, clothes pegs, door latches and mousetraps use small springs.
Mattresses, sofas, cycle seats and charpais are springy so they are comfortable.
Cars, buses, autos and trains have big springs and shock absorbers to soften bumps.
Wind-up watches and clocks run on a coiled spring. HMT made wind-up watches in Bengaluru for decades.
Catapults, bows and slingshots store energy in stretched wood and rubber.
Rubber bands, hair bands and the elastic in clothes hold things snugly.
Balls for cricket, football and tennis are tested for how well they bounce.
Trampolines and diving boards bend and spring back to throw people up.
Bungee cords are bundles of rubber strands that stretch to stop a fall gently.
Musical instruments like the veena, sitar, violin and tabla use stretched strings and skins.
Earthquake-safe buildings are designed to sway and spring back instead of cracking.
Dentists use springy wires, often of memory metal, to straighten teeth. Doctors use springy tubes called stents to hold blood vessels open.
Scientists copy spider silk and resilin to try to make new, tougher materials.
LIGO and the future LIGO-India use the stretching of space to listen to black holes crashing far away.
GPS stations across the Himalaya measure the slow bending of rock, to understand where strain is building before earthquakes.

open_questions.q: What is space made of, that it can stretch and ripple?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure space stretching, but nobody knows what it is made of. String theory and loop quantum gravity are ideas, with no evidence yet.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do spiders make silk that is so strong and so stretchy, and can we make it in factories?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know a lot about the proteins in silk. But copying how the spider spins it, at a large scale, is still very hard.

open_questions.q: Can we predict when bent rock will slip and cause an earthquake?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure rock slowly bending. But they still cannot say when it will slip.

open_questions.q: Why do springs and rubber get 'tired' and crack after being stretched many times?
open_questions.why_open: This is called fatigue. Engineers test it carefully, but exactly when a crack will start is still hard to predict.

open_questions.q: How exactly does titin, the giant spring protein in our muscles, work?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know titin acts like a spring, but how all its parts work together is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can we always see the warning signs before something breaks?
open_questions.why_open: A thing that stays bent is a warning. But tiny cracks can grow inside without showing. Engineers use sound waves and X-rays to look, and still cannot catch everything.

open_questions.q: Could there be a perfectly elastic material that gives back all of its energy?
open_questions.why_open: Every real material turns a little energy into heat each time it springs back. Resilin comes close. Nobody knows how close anything can get.

maths.problem: In the coin stretch test, the thin band was 10 cm long with no coins. Each 5 coins made it 1 cm longer. How long will it be with 30 coins? Use the line graph to help.
maths.explain: 30 coins is 6 lots of 5 coins, because 30 divided by 5 is 6. Each lot adds 1 cm, so the band grows 6 cm. 10 + 6 = 16 cm. On the graph, the line keeps going up 1 cm for every 5 coins.
maths.why_maths: A line graph lets you see the pattern in your stretch results and predict a result you have not measured yet.
maths.context: In the coin stretch test, you hang a paper cup from a rubber band and add coins, 5 at a time. You measure the band each time.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a rubber band as coins are added
chart.note: Each 5 coins made the band about 1 cm longer. The line is straight.

maths.problem: In the coin test, the band's steps for each 5 coins were: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 and a half, and 1 and a half centimetres. Which steps are different from the rest? What might that tell you about the band?
maths.answer: The last two steps are different. They are 1 and a half centimetres instead of 1. When the band was already long, the same 5 coins stretched it more.
maths.explain: The first six steps were all 1 cm, so equal coins gave equal stretches. The last two were half a centimetre bigger. So the band follows the equal-steps rule only up to a point. Rubber follows Hooke's rule only roughly once it is stretched a long way. A steel spring would keep equal steps for longer.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the size of each step, not only at the lengths, shows exactly where a pattern changes.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler beside the rubber band in the picture. The big numbers are centimetres. Each small mark is half a centimetre. The bottom of the band is at the small mark just after 12. How long is the band?
maths.explain: The bottom of the band is past 12 but before 13. It is on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is half a centimetre. So the band is 12 and a half centimetres long.

maths.problem: In the Bungee Doll challenge, 2 bands let the doll fall 30 cm, 3 bands 40 cm and 4 bands 50 cm. The table is 75 cm tall. What is the most bands you can use so the doll's lowest point stays above the floor?
maths.answer: 6 bands. The doll falls 70 cm, which is 5 cm above the floor. 7 bands would be 80 cm, which hits the floor.
maths.explain: Each extra band adds 10 cm. 5 bands make 60 cm. 6 bands make 70 cm. 7 bands make 80 cm. The table is 75 cm tall. 70 cm is less than 75 cm, so 6 bands is safe. 80 cm is more than 75 cm, so 7 bands would hit the floor.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the number pattern in your bungee tests lets you predict a safe jump before you try it.

maths.problem: In the Bounce Test, these balls were dropped from 100 cm. Rubber ball 80 cm, tennis ball 55 cm, sponge ball 20 cm, plastic ball 40 cm. Draw a bar chart. Then answer: how much higher did the rubber ball bounce than the sponge ball?
maths.answer: 60 cm higher. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each ball, as tall as its bounce. The rubber ball bounced 80 cm. The sponge ball bounced 20 cm. 80 take away 20 is 60. So the rubber ball bounced 60 cm higher.
maths.why_maths: After the bounce test you have a list of heights. A bar chart shows the most elastic ball at a glance.

maths.problem: Your rubber band car went 60 cm with 5 winds. Suppose every 5 winds add about the same distance. About how far would it go with 15 winds? Then compare with the real result of 180 cm.
maths.answer: About 180 cm. That matches the real result.
maths.explain: 15 winds is 3 lots of 5 winds. Each lot gives about 60 cm. 3 × 60 = 180 cm. The real car went 180 cm, so the guess was right. With many more winds, the band would reach its limit, and the pattern would stop working.
maths.why_maths: Thinking in equal groups of winds helps you predict how far the car will go before you test it.

maths.problem: One rubber band stretched 4 cm with 20 coins. How far would a chain of 3 of the same bands stretch with the same 20 coins? And how far would 2 bands side by side stretch?
maths.answer: The chain of 3 stretches about 12 cm. The 2 bands side by side stretch about 2 cm.
maths.explain: In a chain, every band carries all 20 coins, so each one stretches 4 cm. 3 lots of 4 cm is 12 cm. Side by side, each band carries half the coins, 10 each. Half the coins gives half the stretch, so 4 divided by 2 is 2 cm.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning with equal groups lets you predict how a new spring will stretch before you build it.

roots.context: We have found that equal pulls give equal stretches, until a spring is pulled too far and stays long. Now we ask what that tells us about the shapes of things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: After a hard pull, your pen spring rested at a new, longer length, and sprang back to that. Nothing outside was stretching it. Its atoms push and pull on each other all the time, and its length is where those forces balance. So a spring lying still is full of forces that cancel out.
deep_truth.habit: We think a thing lying still has no forces in it, and that its length is simply fixed. The pen spring settled at a new length by itself, so something inside it must set its length.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin test experiment, the pen spring came back from small pulls. After a big pull it rested at a new, longer length, and from then on it sprang back to that length.

three.who_am_i: Your body keeps its shape the same way a spring does. Your tendons and skin stretch with every step, then spring back.
three.what_is_life: Living things are full of springs: tendons, spider silk, the rubbery pad in a flea's leg. They store energy when they stretch, and give most of it back for the next step or jump.
three.what_is_this_world: Every solid is a little elastic, even stone and steel. They are just very stiff. The rock under the Himalaya is being bent slowly right now.

roots.thread: A spring lying still has strong pushes and pulls inside it. They cancel out, so the total is zero, and the spring keeps its shape. These pushes and pulls all come from one force, the electric force between atoms. That one force holds the shape of a pen spring, a tendon, a spider's thread and a mountain. Stretch any of them a little, and the same force pulls it back.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus said people do not see how something pulling in two directions can hold together. His examples were the bow and the lyre, a stringed instrument.
teachings.link: A strung bow keeps its shape only because the string pulls one way and the wood pulls back. Inside a solid, each atom stays in place because the pushes and pulls from its neighbours balance.

teachings.teaching: Living plants are soft and bendy. Dead ones are dry and brittle. So the stiff and hard are easily broken, and the soft and bendy last.
teachings.link: In Bend or Snap?, the green twig bends and springs back, and the dry twig snaps. Living tendons, skin and silk are springy too.

teachings.source: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55, the story of Sona
teachings.teaching: The Buddha asks Sona, who once played the veena. If the strings are too tight, does it play in tune? If they are too loose? Only strings stretched just right make music.
teachings.link: In the Rubber Band Orchestra, a band's note changes with how tightly it is stretched. Too loose, and it only thuds. Too tight, and it can pass its limit or snap.

science.text: A solid keeps its shape because of electric pulls and pushes between its atoms. For small stretches, the pull back grows in step with the stretch, which is why Hooke's rule works. Past the elastic limit, rows of atoms slip into new places.
Nobody can yet predict exactly where and when a slip will start, in a bent metal spring or in the rock under the Himalaya.

other_view.who: Aristotle in ancient Greece, and some philosophers today
other_view.view: Aristotle taught that every thing has a form, its own shape and kind, which it keeps by its nature. For him, a spring's shape belongs to what the spring is, not to a balance of pushes and pulls. Some philosophers today still say a thing's form is more than the forces between its parts.

practice.title: Feel two pulls make zero
practice.say: Hold a rubber band between your two pointing fingers. Stretch it a little and keep your hands still. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. The band is not moving. But feel it pull on both fingers, all the time. Now let your fingers come together very slowly. Feel the pull fade as the band goes back. Last, rest your hand on your arm. Your arm is still too. What is pulling inside it?
practice.kid: Stretch a band between two fingers. Keep still. Breathe slowly. Feel it pull both ways. Let it come back slowly.

how_we_found_out.context: Who first found the rule for how springs stretch, and how? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: Robert Hooke was an English scientist. Around 1660, he worked out a rule for how springs stretch. A short wire stretches too little to measure. Hooke hung a pan for weights from a very long wire, 20 to 40 feet long, about 6 to 12 metres. Every part of the wire stretched a tiny amount, and all the tiny amounts added up to a stretch he could measure. He added equal weights, one after another. Each one made the wire longer by about the same step. He tested coiled springs, a watch spring and a strip of dry wood too. In 1676 he hid his rule in a puzzle of jumbled letters, so nobody could claim it first. In 1678 he gave the answer in Latin: 'ut tensio, sic vis'. It means 'as the stretch, so the force'. He said it works for every springy thing, from metal and stone to hair, silk, bone and glass. Later tests showed he had gone too far. Pull anything past its limit, and the steps stop being equal. Rubber follows the rule only roughly. In 1816, Sophie Germain, a French mathematician who taught herself, won a top prize for explaining how springy plates vibrate.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Hooke (1635 to 1703), an English scientist. Later, Sophie Germain (1776 to 1831), a French mathematician.
how_we_found_out.when: He found the rule around 1660, hid it in a letter puzzle in 1676, and published it in 1678.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Hooke said every springy thing follows his rule, however it is stretched. Later tests showed that the rule works only for small stretches, below the elastic limit, and only roughly for rubber.
how_we_found_out.art: Robert Hooke in a 1600s room, a very long wire hanging from a nail high on the wall down to a small pan of weights near the floor, with a pair of compasses measuring the gap to the floor.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today. Coin test: a long, thin rubber band, about 10 cm when hanging, gives steps of about half a centimetre to 1 centimetre for each 5 one-rupee coins. A short or thick band gives steps too small to read, so the unit says to swap it, or cut it into one long strand. The ruler is taped to the same pencil as the band, so it hangs right beside it. A small paper cup holds 40 coins. Homes with few coins can use level tablespoons of rice or dal, one in place of each 5 coins. Many bands give equal steps and then slightly bigger steps near the end, and the unit treats both as honest results. Pen spring: most come back from small pulls, and many stay longer once pulled to about one and a half to two times their length. Springs vary. A grown-up takes the spring out of the pen. The old pen spring jump was replaced by the Band Launch, because a released pen spring flies off in a random direction and its height is hard to read. A band launched off a ruler flies along the floor, and a longer pull clearly sends it further. Two in a Row reuses the coin test set-up, and the chain is measured empty first because two bands start longer. The spine, which is the intro, the coin test, the explanation cards, how we found out, roots and the quiz, fits about 85 to 90 minutes over two sessions.
